pages.title: Letters and speech sounds
pages.c: **Letters belong to writing systems, while speech sounds belong to spoken language.** A familiar letter can lead an English reader toward the wrong pronunciation in another language because spelling conventions are language specific. The Mandarin sentence Wo qu tushuguan and the French question Comment tu t’appelles? use familiar-looking letters, but knowing English spelling does not supply their pronunciations.
support: A writing system can be consistent within one language without providing a universal sound code. Pinyin was designed to represent Mandarin, so its regularity means that its conventions work systematically for Mandarin. It does not mean that an English reader can pronounce its letters by applying English conventions.
pages.d: Pronouncing an unfamiliar language from its spelling requires learning that language’s spelling-to-sound relationships. English, Pinyin, and French can use similar written symbols while assigning them different sound values. This is why a comparison of speech sounds must identify what speakers actually produce rather than treating matching letters as evidence of matching sounds.
pages.visual: The Chinese characters 我去图书馆 and the Pinyin form Wo qu tushuguan represent the same Mandarin expression through different writing systems. The French example adds a second case in which a Roman-letter spelling requires its own pronunciation conventions.

pages.title: A common system for speech sounds
pages.c: **The International Phonetic Alphabet provides a shared system for representing speech sounds across languages.** Its symbols identify properties of pronunciation rather than the spelling conventions of a particular language. This makes it possible to compare two sounds directly even when their ordinary spellings differ, or to distinguish sounds that ordinary writing represents with the same letter.
support: The consonant chart organizes symbols by how the sounds are produced. A symbol’s location therefore carries information about its relationship to neighboring sounds. The chart is useful as a system of comparisons, not just as a list of unfamiliar characters to memorize.
pages.d: The IPA lets researchers describe pronunciation without assuming that one language’s alphabet is the standard. Once sounds have shared labels and an organized classification, a comparison can specify which articulatory properties two sounds share and which property separates them.
pages.visual: The rows and columns group consonants systematically. Plosive, nasal, and fricative appear as row labels, while bilabial, alveolar, and velar appear among the column labels. Symbols occupying related positions represent related patterns of articulation.

pages.title: Place, manner, and voicing
pages.c: **Consonants can be compared by place of articulation, manner of articulation, and voicing.** Place identifies where the vocal tract is constricted. Manner identifies how the airflow is constrained, such as by a complete closure for a plosive or a narrower passage for a fricative. Voicing concerns the timing of vocal-fold vibration relative to the articulation.
support: The IPA chart places progressively farther-back articulations across its columns. Its rows separate different ways of controlling airflow. Within a paired position, the right-hand symbol represents the voiced member. A sound can therefore share two of these properties with another sound while differing on the third.
pages.d: Classifying a consonant means locating the constriction, describing what that constriction does to airflow, and identifying the voicing pattern. These are separate dimensions. Two consonants can be produced at the lips in the same manner and still differ in when vocal-fold vibration occurs.
pages.visual: Bilabial sounds appear toward the left of the chart because their constriction occurs at the lips. Velar and more posterior articulations appear farther right. The paired p and b symbols occupy the plosive row in the bilabial column.

pages.title: Comparing p and b
pages.c: **/p/ and /b/ share their place and manner of articulation but contrast in voicing.** Both are bilabial plosives, so the lips make a closure that is subsequently released. Their contrast concerns the timing of phonation around that closure and release. Treating them as related feature combinations explains both their similarity and their difference.
support: The same kind of voicing comparison applies to /t/ and /d/. Although that pair is produced at a different place, it shares the relation between a voiceless and a voiced stop. Features therefore allow a general statement about voiced stops such as /b/, /d/, and /g/, rather than a separate unrelated description for every consonant.
pages.d: Changing /p/ into /b/ preserves the bilabial closure and the stop manner while changing the voicing category. A feature description makes that relationship explicit. It also connects this particular pair to other stop pairs that contrast on the same dimension.
pages.visual: The two feature lists both mark plosive and bilabial positively. Their voiced entries differ. The visual alignment of the lists isolates the feature responsible for the contrast.

pages.title: Aspiration and language-specific stop contrasts
pages.c: **The phonetic realization of a voicing contrast depends on the language and the speaking context.** In the English examples peer and beer, the initial contrast can involve an aspirated [pʰ] and an unaspirated [p]. Aspiration is the puff of air after the closure is released. Holding a hand in front of the mouth makes the difference in airflow easier to notice.
support: The French examples pou and boue illustrate a different realization, with [p] contrasting against voiced [b]. Thus, the same broad labels of voiced and voiceless stops do not guarantee identical timing patterns across languages. The narrow IPA symbols keep these particular pronunciations distinct.
pages.d: An English /p/ can be produced with a substantial puff after release, while an English /b/ can begin without continuous voicing during its closure. French can implement its contrast with a different voicing pattern. The phonemic distinction and the detailed physical realization must therefore be described at different levels.
pages.visual: The superscript h in [pʰ] marks aspiration. The feature lists distinguish [pʰ] from [p] through aspiration, while [b] is marked voiced. These are three distinguishable phones, even though a language may organize them into fewer contrastive categories.

pages.title: Broad and narrow transcription
pages.c: **Slashes and square brackets distinguish phonemic categories from detailed phonetic realizations.** A broad transcription such as /p/ identifies the phoneme used in a language. A narrow transcription such as [pʰ] records more detail about how that sound was actually produced. The two notations answer different questions about the same utterance.
support: Broad transcription emphasizes the distinctions that organize words in the language. Narrow transcription can preserve differences such as aspiration even when those differences do not distinguish words. Recording more phonetic detail does not automatically create more phonemes.
pages.d: /p/ names a category in a phonological description, whereas [pʰ] specifies an aspirated physical realization. Square brackets are useful when comparing fine differences between pronunciations. Slashes are useful when identifying the sound categories that distinguish lexical forms.
pages.visual: The broad /p/ and /b/ labels appear beside more detailed [pʰ], [p], and [b] descriptions. The contrast between two broad labels and three narrow forms makes clear why a phone and a phoneme are not interchangeable terms.

pages.title: Place of articulation in the vocal tract
pages.c: **Place of articulation describes a physical constriction in the vocal tract.** The lips can close together, and different parts of the tongue can approach or contact different regions of the mouth. These movements change where the outward airflow is interrupted or narrowed. The feature labels are grounded in those bodily actions.
support: A bilabial closure uses both lips. Tongue-based articulations instead depend on which part of the tongue approaches which surface. Comparing the location of contact separates place from manner, since complete closure can occur at several different places.
pages.d: Consonant categories refer to coordinated articulatory movements. To identify place, locate the main constriction rather than relying on the written letter. Different closures can use different articulators while sharing the same general stop manner.
pages.visual: The left drawing closes the upper and lower lips, locating a bilabial constriction at the front of the mouth. The middle drawing raises the tongue tip toward the ridge behind the upper teeth, showing an alveolar constriction. The right drawing raises the back of the tongue toward the soft palate, showing a velar constriction.

pages.title: Nasal airflow and constrictions at the teeth
pages.c: **Consonant features describe both the route of airflow and the articulators that create a constriction.** A nasal consonant allows air through the nose while the mouth is closed at some point. Other consonants involve a constriction where the lower lip meets the upper teeth or where the tongue approaches the teeth. These are different physical arrangements within the same vocal tract.
support: Nasal airflow depends on the opening between the oral and nasal passages. A nasal consonant can therefore share its oral place of articulation with a stop while differing in the route available to the air.

Labiodental describes a constriction involving the lower lip and upper teeth. Dental describes one involving the tongue and teeth. Identifying the participating articulators explains the place label instead of tying it to a written letter.
pages.d: Track the airflow and locate the constriction as separate steps. Opening the nasal passage lets air continue through the nose despite a closure in the mouth. For labiodental and dental articulations, the relevant difference lies at the front of the mouth, where either the lower lip or the tongue approaches the teeth.
pages.visual: The left drawing combines closed lips with an open route toward the nasal cavity. The middle drawing brings the lower lip against the upper teeth, a labiodental configuration. The right drawing positions the tongue at the front teeth, a dental configuration. Each diagram identifies a different part of the articulatory description.

pages.title: Vowel height, backness, and rounding
pages.c: **Vowels are organized by height, frontness or backness, and lip rounding.** Close vowels generally involve a higher tongue position and a less open jaw than open vowels. Front vowels place the tongue body farther forward than back vowels. Rounding adds a further distinction because the lips can change shape while the tongue remains in a similar region.
support: The vowel /y/ in French tu and Mandarin qu is a useful example. Starting from /i/ and rounding the lips changes the vowel toward /y/ without requiring the back-tongue position associated with /u/. This separates a change in lip shape from a change in tongue position.
pages.d: A vowel description combines several articulatory dimensions. Front versus back concerns tongue placement, close versus open concerns height, and rounded versus unrounded concerns the lips. The /i/ to /y/ comparison is informative because it changes rounding while retaining a close front configuration.
pages.visual: The vowel chart runs from close at the top to open at the bottom and from front at the left to back at the right. Where symbols are paired, the right-hand member is rounded. Thus i and y occupy the same high front region but differ in lip rounding.

pages.title: Vowels involve changing articulatory configurations
pages.c: **A vowel category describes a pattern of articulation rather than one permanently fixed tongue shape.** Tongue position helps distinguish vowels, but the whole vocal tract contributes to the sound. Some vowels also change substantially during their production. The diphthongs in boat and bait involve movement through time rather than a single sustained configuration.
support: The plotted tongue-body centers summarize one important difference among vowels. They are useful reference points, but a point cannot represent the entire tongue contour or its trajectory. A dynamic vowel is understood by following the change in configuration over its duration.
pages.d: Vowels can be compared using tongue-body position, but speaking produces moving configurations. A diphthong such as the vowel in boat changes as the syllable unfolds. A static location is therefore a useful description of part of the articulation rather than a complete picture of the spoken event.
pages.visual: The colored contours represent different tongue shapes, and the dots identify tongue-body centers. Several contours can differ beyond the location of a single dot, showing why the diagram uses both whole outlines and summary points.

pages.title: Dialect differences in vowel contrasts
pages.c: **Speakers of the same language can differ in which vowels they distinguish.** For the instructor’s mid-Atlantic New York variety, caught and cot have different vowels. Many other American English speakers pronounce those words alike. A difference that is present in one dialect can therefore be absent in another without preventing the speakers from using English.
support: A vowel chart organizes categories, but the inventory must be interpreted for a particular speech variety. The two lower back positions are especially relevant to the caught–cot example. Establishing whether a speaker distinguishes them requires listening to that speaker rather than assuming a single inventory for every American English speaker.
pages.d: Caught and cot test whether a speaker maintains a particular low-back vowel contrast. A speaker who produces different vowels has two distinguishable forms here. A speaker with the merger produces them as homophones. The difference is a systematic dialect pattern, not simply a pronunciation mistake.
pages.visual: The simplified chart separates a rounded low-back vowel from the open back /ɑ/ position. The contrast between these neighboring regions is the one illustrated by caught and cot for the instructor’s dialect.

pages.title: The lack of invariance problem
pages.c: **The same speech category can have different acoustic realizations across speakers and contexts.** Listeners nevertheless understand speech, including dialect differences such as speakers who merge the vowels in Aaron and Erin. The lack of invariance problem asks how a stable linguistic interpretation can be recovered from a signal whose physical properties vary.
support: The vowel distributions contain substantial spread within each labeled category, and neighboring categories overlap. Identifying a vowel cannot therefore mean checking whether its first and second formants equal one fixed pair of values. The listener has to interpret variable acoustic evidence as language.
pages.d: Variation is part of ordinary speech perception. Different productions of one vowel do not occupy a single acoustic point, and the ranges for different vowels can overlap. The central problem is explaining how listeners recognize categories despite this variability.
pages.visual: The horizontal axis gives the frequency of the first formant, F1, and the vertical axis gives the second formant, F2, in cycles per second. Repeated vowel symbols spread across the plot, while the enclosing regions summarize their distributions. The overlap makes the absence of a unique acoustic signature visible.

pages.title: Minimal pairs establish phonemic contrast
pages.c: **A minimal pair consists of two words whose difference in meaning depends on a difference in one speech sound in the same context.** Such a pair establishes that the sounds are contrastive for that language or dialect. When substituting one phone for another distinguishes words, the distinction is represented phonemically.
support: Caught and cot serve this purpose for a speaker who distinguishes their vowels. The surrounding consonants remain the same, so the vowel difference carries the contrast. For a speaker who merges those vowels, that particular pair does not establish two vowel phonemes in the same way.
pages.d: To demonstrate a phonemic distinction, find a word pair in which changing the sound changes the word while the rest of the relevant form stays the same. The evidence is the contrast in meaning, not just the fact that two pronunciations sound different.
pages.visual: The written comparison concerns two low-back vowels, while the accompanying minimal-pair discussion focuses attention on the relationship between sound and lexical meaning. The critical evidence is a controlled word contrast.

pages.title: Minimal pairs reveal shared contrastive features
pages.c: **Minimal pairs can show that several consonant contrasts depend on the same feature.** In English, /b/ and /p/, /d/ and /t/, and /g/ and /k/ differ in voicing. Each pair holds place and stop manner constant while changing the voicing category. Comparing the pairs makes the shared dimension clear.
support: The relevant evidence must come from the language being analyzed. The physical existence of two phones does not by itself show that they form a phonemic contrast in every language. Minimal pairs connect a particular sound distinction with a difference between words.
pages.d: A feature such as voicing provides a general description across several minimal-pair contrasts. Bilabial, alveolar, and velar stops occur at different places, yet the voiced–voiceless relationship can recur at each place. Minimal pairs show that this relationship matters for distinguishing English words.
pages.visual: The listed pairs align a voiced stop with a voiceless stop at the same place of articulation. This parallel arrangement separates the feature that changes within a pair from the place that changes across pairs.

pages.title: Allophones are realizations of one phoneme
pages.c: **Allophones are different phonetic realizations of the same phoneme.** A speaker can produce /p/ differently depending on its position and neighboring sounds without changing the underlying word contrast. Some of this variation is predictable from the phonological context, making it systematic rather than random noise.
support: The phrases pot that, spot that, and stop that place /p/ in different environments. Comparing recordings allows the release and aspiration patterns to be examined while the target consonant remains a realization of /p/. The question is how pronunciation changes with context, not whether every phonetic difference creates a new word.
pages.d: One phoneme can cover several distinguishable phones. The different /p/ realizations in pot, spot, and stop illustrate how surrounding segments and syllable position affect pronunciation. Allophony describes this organized variation within a phonemic category.
pages.visual: The three phrases change the position of /p/ relative to /s/ and the vowel. This creates a comparison among initial, post-/s/, and final positions while retaining the same broad consonant category.

pages.title: Reading the allophone comparison
pages.c: **A speech recording makes differences among /p/ realizations observable in time.** The pot, spot, and stop comparison places the consonant in different contexts, so the timing of closure, release, aspiration, and the following voiced sound can differ. These physical differences are compatible with the words containing the same phoneme /p/.
support: A waveform displays changes in the sound signal’s amplitude over time. A spectrogram displays the distribution of acoustic energy over time and frequency. Looking at both representations helps relate abrupt releases and quieter intervals to the surrounding stretches of speech.
pages.d: The three recorded phrases provide comparable acoustic windows onto contextual variation. Different release and aspiration patterns are meaningful phonetic observations, but a decision about phoneme identity also depends on whether a difference distinguishes words in that language.
pages.visual: The upper panel is the waveform, and the lower panel is the spectrogram. Time runs horizontally in both, so corresponding events align vertically. The lower panel’s vertical axis is frequency, allowing changes in the distribution of sound energy to be compared across the phrases.

pages.title: Release differences without a meaning contrast
pages.c: **An unreleased [p̚] and an aspirated [pʰ] can both occur in English stop without changing the word’s meaning.** A clearly released or aspirated final consonant may occur in careful speech or when the word is stressed. Because this contrast does not establish separate words in those contexts, the two phones are treated as allophones of /p/.
support: The forms stop, stops, stopped, and stopping provide additional contexts in which the realization of /p/ can change. Adding material after the consonant changes its environment. The phonetic behavior of the consonant is therefore related to the form in which the word occurs.
pages.d: Audible pronunciation differences do not automatically correspond to different phonemes. Saying stop with a final release and saying it without an audible release can communicate the same word. Allophony captures this difference in physical realization while preserving the shared phonemic category.
pages.visual: The small unreleased-stop mark in [p̚] distinguishes it from the superscript h in [pʰ]. These marks add phonetic detail inside square brackets. The shared word interpretation is what makes the two forms an allophonic example.

pages.title: Two uses of the term voicing
pages.c: **Voicing can refer either to a phonetic property or to a phonological contrast.** In a narrow description of a particular phone, voiced means that the vocal folds vibrate during the relevant sound or gesture. In a broad description, a voicing contrast can be realized through several context-dependent acoustic and articulatory differences.
support: Word-initial aspiration can help distinguish the English stop categories even when the physical realization is not a simple vibration-versus-no-vibration contrast throughout the closure. The writer–rider example likewise directs attention to relative timing of voicing and closure. A phonological label summarizes a language’s contrast, while a narrow transcription specifies the actual realization.
pages.d: Ask which level is being described when you encounter the word voiced. A phonetic claim concerns actual vocal-fold vibration in a specific production. A phonemic claim concerns the contrast between categories, whose physical cues can vary with the context.
pages.visual: The distinction is organized around broad versus narrow transcription. Examples involving initial aspiration and writer–rider timing demonstrate why a single phonological contrast can involve more than one measurable cue.

pages.title: Phonotactics constrain syllable patterns
pages.c: **Phonotactics concerns which sound combinations a language permits and how they fit into syllables.** English speakers can alter unfamiliar consonant clusters when pronouncing borrowed words or names. The adjustments reflect the patterns of English syllables rather than a simple inability to articulate each individual consonant.
support: The name Sbarro can be produced with an initial [sp] or [zb] sequence rather than the written-looking [sb] combination. Names such as Zbigniew and Gbagbo can prompt inserted vowels that break difficult clusters into syllables. The pattern of permitted combinations shapes production at a level above individual sounds.
pages.d: Knowing a language includes knowing its possible sound sequences. When an incoming name contains a cluster that does not fit familiar syllable patterns, a speaker may change a consonant or insert a vowel. The result makes the sequence fit the speaker’s phonological system more readily.
pages.visual: The written name Sbarro contrasts with the bracketed pronunciations [spɑroʊ] and [zbɑroʊ]. The inserted vowels in the other transcriptions make additional syllabic structure visible. The spelling alone does not predict the exact sequence that an English speaker produces.

pages.title: A phoneme is a contrastive unit
pages.c: **A phoneme is a smallest sound unit capable of distinguishing meaning within a language.** It is defined by its role in contrasts, not by being a letter or one unchanging physical sound. A phoneme can therefore have several allophones while remaining one category in the language’s system of word distinctions.
support: The IPA gives researchers a precise notation for similarities and differences among speech sounds. Its symbols are especially useful when identifying phones and their features. Treating that notation as an ordinary alphabet would obscure the distinction between a written symbol, a specific production, and a language’s contrastive category.
pages.d: Letters, phones, and phonemes belong to different descriptions. A letter is part of a writing system, a phone is a speech realization, and a phoneme organizes meaning-bearing contrasts. This distinction explains why the number of written symbols, physical variants, and phonemes can differ.
pages.visual: The definition centers on a distinction in meaning. That criterion connects phonemes to minimal-pair evidence, while the discussion of variable gestures connects them to the need to recognize allophones.

pages.title: Continuous speech is not a row of letters
pages.c: **Speech is a continuously changing acoustic signal, not a sequence of neatly separated letter-like packages.** In A sore back is a real pain, successive articulations influence the signal as the utterance unfolds. A phonemic transcription provides useful categories, but those categories do not correspond to isolated blocks with identical acoustic shapes in every context.
support: The spectrogram makes the contrast between a categorical description and a continuous signal visible. Broad frequency patterns change over time, and transitions connect neighboring segments. Recognizing the sentence involves interpreting those changing patterns rather than locating a clean boundary around each written letter.
pages.d: A transcription breaks an utterance into symbols for analysis. The sound itself contains overlapping and context-dependent information. The important distinction is between the discrete symbols in the representation and the continuous physical event those symbols describe.
pages.visual: Time runs from left to right, frequency increases vertically, and dark regions indicate stronger acoustic energy. The phonetic labels and red boundary markers are annotations above the acoustic display. They organize the interpretation of the signal rather than turning it into separate physical tiles.

pages.title: The moving vocal tract
pages.c: **Speech requires coordinated movements of the lips, jaw, tongue, and other structures of the vocal tract.** Their changing configuration shapes the outgoing sound. Because these movements occur as an ongoing sequence, a speech gesture belongs to a moving system rather than an isolated posture repeated unchanged for every occurrence of a phoneme.
support: A side view of the vocal tract helps connect acoustic speech with the structures that produce it. The tongue changes the internal shape of the oral cavity, while the lips and jaw change its opening. The configuration of these parts jointly matters for the sound.
pages.d: Producing an utterance involves shaping the vocal tract continuously. The tongue and lips work together with the jaw rather than independently stamping out one letter-like sound at a time. Articulatory views make the physical basis of this coordination concrete.
pages.visual: The USC SPAN side view locates the tongue within the mouth and the passage extending toward the throat. The outline of the lips and the tongue’s position connect the spoken output to the configuration of the vocal tract.

pages.title: Hockett’s overlapping-eggs analogy
pages.c: **Hockett’s 1955 analogy explains why recognizing speech differs from recovering a sequence of separate physical pieces.** Eggs enter a wringer as distinguishable objects, but their contents mix as they pass through. The listener is compared to an inspector who uses the mixed remains to identify which eggs were originally present.
support: The analogy maps the distinguishable eggs onto an intended sequence and the mixed output onto the speech signal after production. Information about neighboring elements spreads together. The inspector’s job is identification from the resulting pattern, not physically rebuilding each original egg.
pages.d: Overlapping acoustic information can still support recognition. Hockett’s listener identifies the original elements from a mixture whose parts are no longer cleanly separated. The example highlights the difference between a discrete linguistic description and the combined physical consequences of speaking.
pages.visual: The egg colors, yolks, whites, and shell fragments stand for different traces of the original elements. Their mixture explains why perceptual identification does not require perfectly separating and reconstructing every original physical unit.

pages.title: Phonemes as a question about representation
pages.c: **The usefulness of a phonemic description raises a further question about representation.** A category can help linguists describe contrasts without settling exactly how a speaker stores words or how a listener recognizes speech. Research therefore asks whether phoneme-sized units are the right description of the mental processes themselves.
support: The cited work includes questions about phonological categories in lexical learning, word storage beyond phones and phonemes, and the psychological interpretation of phoneme representations. These are questions about what the linguistic categories correspond to in learning, memory, and perception.
pages.d: A successful descriptive notation and a model of mental processing answer related but different questions. Phonemic categories describe sound contrasts. A psychological account must also explain how experience, word knowledge, and the variable speech signal support recognition and production.
pages.visual: The cited titles focus on the illusion of the phoneme, the development of phonological categories in lexical learning, and word storage beyond phones and phonemes. Their common issue is the relation between analytic categories and actual cognitive representation.

questions.stem: Why does a regular Pinyin spelling system still pose a problem for an English reader?
choices: Its consistent letter–sound conventions are Mandarin conventions, which the English reader may not know.
Regular spelling means that every letter has the same sound in every language.
Pinyin uses phonemic categories that are identical to English letters.
Any regular spelling system necessarily omits pronunciation information.
questions.why: Regularity within a writing system does not make its symbols universal. Familiar-looking letters can have different sound values across languages.

questions.stem: Which comparison keeps place and manner constant while changing the voicing category?
choices: /p/ versus /b/
/p/ versus /t/
/p/ versus /m/
/i/ versus /y/
questions.why: Both /p/ and /b/ are bilabial plosives. /p/–/t/ changes place, /p/–/m/ changes manner, and /i/–/y/ illustrates vowel rounding.

questions.stem: What does the contrast between /p/ and [pʰ] identify?
choices: A phonemic category versus a more detailed aspirated phonetic realization.
A written English letter versus a written French letter.
Two phonemes that must distinguish words in every language.
A voiced sound versus a sound that contains no consonant closure.
questions.why: Slashes indicate a broad phonemic representation, while brackets specify phonetic detail. The superscript h marks aspiration.

questions.stem: Starting from /i/ and rounding the lips toward /y/ helps isolate which vowel property?
choices: Lip rounding while retaining a close front tongue configuration.
A change from a front vowel to a back vowel in every case.
A change from a vowel to a bilabial stop.
A change from a phoneme to a written letter.
questions.why: The /i/–/y/ comparison separates rounding from tongue backness. Both occupy the close front region of the vowel chart.

questions.stem: What aspect of the F1–F2 vowel plot illustrates the lack of invariance problem?
choices: Productions within vowel categories vary, and the category distributions overlap.
Every vowel has one exact F1–F2 coordinate for all speakers.
F1 is a time axis that directly divides the signal into letters.
The ellipses identify the written spellings used in different countries.
questions.why: The plot represents first- and second-formant frequencies. Spread and overlap make a simple one-category-to-one-fixed-acoustic-point rule inadequate.

questions.stem: What does caught versus cot demonstrate for a speaker who produces different vowels in those words?
choices: A minimal pair in which the vowel difference distinguishes lexical meanings.
Two spellings of the same word that cannot establish a sound contrast.
An allophonic alternation because different meanings are irrelevant.
A contrast that must be present in every American English dialect.
questions.why: The surrounding consonants are held constant and the words differ in their vowels and meanings. Speakers with a merger do not maintain this contrast.

questions.stem: Why can final [p̚] and [pʰ] in stop be treated as allophones in the described English contexts?
choices: The phonetic difference does not distinguish different word meanings in those contexts.
The two productions have completely identical acoustic signals.
An aspirated sound can never occur at the end of a word.
Square brackets always indicate separate phonemes.
questions.why: The two phones differ in release and aspiration, but the word remains stop. Lack of a lexical contrast is central to this allophonic analysis.

questions.stem: An English speaker inserts vowels when attempting an unfamiliar initial consonant cluster. Which concept best explains the pattern?
choices: Phonotactic constraints on familiar syllable structures.
A minimal pair proving the inserted vowels are silent letters.
The claim that every written consonant corresponds to one invariant gesture.
A change in the semantic roles of the sentence.
questions.why: Phonotactics governs permitted sound combinations. Vowel insertion can adapt an unfamiliar cluster to a familiar syllable pattern.

questions.stem: Why are the phonetic labels above the sentence spectrogram not equivalent to separate physical tiles in the signal?
choices: The signal changes continuously and contains context-dependent transitions across neighboring sounds.
The spectrogram contains only written language and no sound measurements.
The frequency axis records the order of letters in the alphabet.
Each label guarantees an identical acoustic pattern in every occurrence.
questions.why: The transcription categorizes speech, while the spectrogram represents its continuous acoustic realization. Annotations do not make the sound physically discrete.

questions.stem: What is the listener’s task in Hockett’s egg analogy?
choices: Identify the original elements from mixed traces left by their combined output.
Reassemble every original physical egg before recognizing anything.
Ignore all overlap and read an ordinary orthographic transcript.
Assign each phoneme a single acoustic value that cannot vary.
questions.why: The inspector identifies the eggs from mixed remnants. The analogy emphasizes recognition despite overlap rather than literal physical reconstruction.

written.prompt: Explain how minimal pairs distinguish phonemic contrast from allophonic variation, using the caught–cot and stop examples.
answer: For speakers who distinguish caught and cot, a vowel difference in the same consonant context distinguishes words and meanings.
Released or aspirated and unreleased final /p/ in stop can preserve the same word meaning, so the phones can be allophones in those English contexts.
A physical difference alone is insufficient to establish a phonemic contrast.

written.prompt: Explain the lack of invariance problem using the vowel plot, the continuous-speech spectrogram, and Hockett’s analogy.
answer: The formant plot contains spread within vowel categories and overlap between them.
The spectrogram represents a continuous and context-dependent acoustic signal rather than identical isolated blocks for successive phonemes.
Hockett’s inspector identifies original elements from mixed evidence, illustrating recognition without physical reconstruction of separate units.
